title: Given an unsorted array of integers and a value K, return the Kth largest element (by value, not the Kth distinct element).
shortTitle: Kth Largest Element in an Array — min-heap of size K or QuickSelect

s1_definition.profdef: Two efficient techniques solve this. A min-heap of size K keeps only the K largest elements seen so far, so its smallest element, the heap root, is the Kth largest overall after one pass. QuickSelect partitions the array around a pivot like quicksort but recurses into only the side containing the target rank, giving average linear time.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine finding the tenth-largest deposit of the day. The heap approach keeps a shortlist of exactly the ten biggest deposits seen so far; whenever a bigger deposit arrives, it bumps out the smallest on the shortlist, and at the end the smallest on that shortlist is the tenth-largest. QuickSelect instead picks a sample deposit, splits the rest into bigger and smaller piles, and keeps narrowing to the pile that must contain the rank you want.
s1_definition.oneliner: Keep a size-K min-heap whose root is the Kth largest (O(n log K)), or use QuickSelect to partition toward the target rank in average O(n).
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Two efficient techniques solve this. A min-heap of size K keeps only the K largest elements seen so far, so its smallest element, the heap root, is the Kth largest overall after one pass. QuickSelect partitions the array around a pivot like quicksort but recurses into only the side containing the target rank, giving average linear time.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine finding the tenth-largest deposit of the day. The heap approach keeps a shortlist of exactly the ten biggest deposits seen so far; whenever a bigger deposit arrives, it bumps out the smallest on the shortlist, and at the end the smallest on that shortlist is the tenth-largest. QuickSelect instead picks a sample deposit, splits the rest into bigger and smaller piles, and keeps narrowing to the pile that must contain the rank you want.

**One line to remember:** Keep a size-K min-heap whose root is the Kth largest (O(n log K)), or use QuickSelect to partition toward the target rank in average O(n).

sections.s2_technical:
The min-heap approach pushes each element and, whenever the heap size exceeds K, removes the smallest. This keeps exactly the K largest elements, so the root is the Kth largest. For example: `heap.offer(x); if (heap.size() > K) heap.poll();` then `return heap.peek();`. The time is n log K and the extra space is K.

QuickSelect treats the problem as finding the element at index n minus K in sorted order. It chooses a pivot, partitions the array so smaller elements go left and larger go right, and checks where the pivot landed. For example: `int p = partition(a, lo, hi);` then compare `p` with the target index.

If the pivot index equals the target, that element is the answer. If the target is to the left, recurse left; otherwise recurse right. Because only one side is explored, the average cost is linear, though a bad pivot sequence can degrade to quadratic, which randomized pivoting mitigates. For example: swap a random index into the pivot position before partitioning.

A senior nuance is the trade-off: the heap is simple, stable in worst case at n log K, and ideal for streaming because it processes elements one at a time, while QuickSelect is faster on average at linear time but mutates the array and has a quadratic worst case unless the pivot is randomized. The choice depends on whether data arrives as a stream and whether in-place mutation is acceptable.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, the risk desk needs the Kth largest transaction amount of the day to set an alert threshold. The system must compute this from an unsorted list of amounts. This is exactly how Kth Largest works — it returns the element at the target rank.

Problem 2 — Amounts arrive continuously during the day, so a streaming-friendly method that holds only K values is preferred over sorting everything. This is exactly why the size-K min-heap is used here, with QuickSelect noted as the in-memory alternative.

The mini-project builds a `KthLargestFinder` service with both a heap method and a QuickSelect method, a `BankLogFormatter`, and a runnable demo.

sections.s5_journey:
The input amounts are 5000, 12000, 800, 25000, 3000, 17500, 9000 with K equal to three.

Step 1: The heap method pushes 5000, 12000, 800, filling a heap of size three with those values.

Step 2: It pushes 25000, size becomes four, so it removes the smallest which is 800, leaving 5000, 12000, 25000.

Step 3: It pushes 3000, removes the new smallest 3000, so the heap still holds 5000, 12000, 25000.

Step 4: It pushes 17500, removes 5000, leaving 12000, 17500, 25000. It pushes 9000, removes 9000, leaving 12000, 17500, 25000. The root is 12000, the third largest.

Step 5: QuickSelect targets index seven minus three equals four in ascending order. Sorted, the array is 800, 3000, 5000, 9000, 12000, 17500, 25000, and index four is 12000.

Step 6: QuickSelect partitions around random pivots, recursing only into the side holding index four, and returns 12000 without fully sorting. Both methods agree on 12000.

```text
2026-10-26T20:50:00Z [INFO] National Bank of India — Kth Largest Transaction Amount
2026-10-26T20:50:00Z [INFO] Kth largest (heap) k=3 -> 12000
2026-10-26T20:50:00Z [INFO] Kth largest (quickselect) k=3 -> 12000
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Finding the Kth largest element has two strong solutions, and I pick between them based on context. The size-K min-heap keeps only the K largest elements seen so far: I push each element and, whenever the heap grows past K, I remove the smallest. After one pass the heap root is the Kth largest, because exactly the K biggest values remain and the root is the smallest of those. This runs in n log K time with K extra space and is ideal when data arrives as a stream, since it consumes elements one at a time.

QuickSelect is the in-memory alternative and is faster on average. I reframe the question as finding the element at index n minus K in ascending sorted order, then partition the array around a pivot like quicksort but recurse into only the side that contains that target index. Because I discard one side each step, the average cost is linear. The catch is a bad pivot sequence can degrade to quadratic, so I randomize the pivot to make that practically impossible.

The trade-off is what interviewers want: the heap is simple, worst-case n log K, streaming-friendly, and leaves the input untouched; QuickSelect is average linear but mutates the array and needs randomization to avoid the quadratic worst case. Stating that trade-off clearly is the senior signal.

In my project at National Bank of India, the risk desk set a daily alert threshold from the Kth largest transaction amount. Because amounts streamed in all day, I used the size-K min-heap so the system held only K values at any moment and produced the threshold in a single pass, keeping QuickSelect as the option for batch recomputation over a finished day's data held fully in memory.
